analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug-benefit middlemen to report drug prices, fees, and side payments to health plans.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved it 44-0 with bipartisan sponsorship, but the bill never got a House floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are the middlemen that negotiate drug prices and manage prescription benefits for Medicare drug plans, and their fees and side arrangements are largely hidden. This bill would require PBMs to give the plans they serve an annual, itemized report: every drug dispensed, what it cost, what rebates were collected, what revenue the PBM and its affiliated pharmacies kept, and when the PBM steered fills to its own pharmacies or favored a brand drug over a cheaper generic. It would also let the plans audit the PBM every year, make PBMs pay any fines caused by their own failures, and order a study of redundant reporting rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and the drug plans that cover them. Plans would get the data to see when a PBM is overcharging or steering prescriptions to its own pharmacies, which would let them renegotiate or switch PBMs. Independent community pharmacies would benefit indirectly when plans can see the price gap between PBM-affiliated pharmacies and everyone else. Taxpayers also benefit, since Medicare covers a large share of drug costs that are inflated by opaque PBM fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare drug-plan enrollees and community pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: PBMs must submit an annual itemized report to each drug plan covering every drug dispensed, total rebates and other manufacturer payments, the revenue the PBM and its affiliates retained, and gross versus net plan spending [S2][S3].

Where a PBM owns a pharmacy, it must disclose what share of prescriptions went to its own pharmacies and how prices there compare with non-affiliated pharmacies in the network, exposing self-dealing [S3].

Plans can audit the PBM at least yearly, pick the auditor without PBM-imposed limits, and PBMs must reimburse plans for any federal fine caused by PBM noncompliance, plus face contract penalties [S3].
Plans must report when a brand drug gets better coverage than competing generics or biosimilars, along with written justification and the estimated cost difference to beneficiaries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The three dominant PBMs and their parent companies (which also own insurance arms and pharmacy chains) bear the cost of gathering and filing the reports and the risk of exposed margins. Medicare drug-plan sponsors take on modest new certification duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large pharmacy benefit managers and their parent companies

drawbacks.text: The disclosures are not public. The bill's confidentiality section forbids the government from releasing information that identifies a specific PBM or prices for specific drugs, so this is transparency for plan sponsors and auditors, not for beneficiaries or shoppers comparing pharmacies [S3].

The bill requires reporting and audits but bans no PBM practice. It does not prohibit spread pricing, the steering of fills to affiliated pharmacies, or PBM pay tied to a drug's list price; it assumes plans will use the new data to police the middlemen themselves [S2][S3].

Compliance costs fall on PBMs and plan sponsors, and the bill adds a Government Accountability Office study of overlapping federal and state reporting rules, which its own text treats as a burden worth streamlining [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries this is a real but indirect gain: the bill does not directly lower any drug price, it arms plan sponsors with the information to squeeze PBMs, and the pressure would take years to show up in premiums and copays. The main honest criticism is that the public never gets to see the numbers, so the sunlight reaches only the plans and regulators who already had leverage. The compliance burden is real for PBMs and their corporate parents, which is precisely the point.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote in November 2023 and won a unanimous 44-0 committee vote in December 2023, but House leadership never brought it up for a floor vote before the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Landsman (D-OH) and Rep. Diana Harshbarger (R-TN) introduced the bill on September 12, 2023, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees [S1][S5].
The Health Subcommittee considered and marked it up on November 15, 2023, forwarding it to the full committee by voice vote [S5].
The full committee ordered the bill reported as amended on December 6, 2023, by a vote of 44-0 [S5].
After that committee vote, no further floor action occurred in the House and the bill was never voted on before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large pharmacy benefit managers. They never had to file the annual reports or open their books to plan-sponsored audits, so their fee arrangements, rebate retention, and affiliated-pharmacy steering stay undisclosed, and the drug prices built on those arrangements remain in place.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored it with a Republican cosponsor, and the full committee ordered it reported 44-0 with no member voting no.

industries.note: PBMs would have to disclose annually what they charge plans, what manufacturer rebates they keep, and how much business goes to their own pharmacies, plus submit to plan-chosen audits and absorb fines for noncompliance. This threatens the fee and spread income that opaque reporting protects, and their loss runs with the public's gain.

The bill forces disclosure of the price gap and prescription share between PBM-affiliated pharmacies and independent ones in each network. That makes it harder to steer fills to affiliated stores, which is a persistent complaint of independent pharmacists.

Plans must report whenever a brand drug receives better coverage than competing generics or biosimilars, with written justification, which pressures manufacturers that pay for favorable formulary placement. But the bill mandates no coverage changes, so existing arrangements continue.
